title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
raw_text: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
raw_text: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
raw_text: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: U

title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). title: The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
raw_text: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
raw_text: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán

title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
raw_text: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth. Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. title: Forse Vlaamse besparingen treffen erfgoedbibliotheken, archieven en kwetsbare lezers hard
raw_text: De drastische besparingsplannen van de nieuwe Vlaamse regering slaan diepe wonden in de archief- en bibliotheeksector. Naast het nieuws dat landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken hun volledige structurele subsidies verliezen en archieven de helft moeten inleveren, luiden nu ook de informatieopleidingen en de sector voor passend lezen de noodklok. In twee brandbrieven waarschuwen de Arteveldehogeschool en Luisterpuntbibliotheek voor onomkeerbare schade aan het Vlaamse geheugen en de toegankelijkheid van informatie. Ook de VVBAD (Vlaamse Vereniging voor Bibliotheek, Archief & Documentatie ), Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge , Universiteitsbibliotheek Gent en Erfgoedbibliotheek Hendrik Conscience roepen op tot actie. Binnen het nieuwe begrotingsakkoord van minister van Cultuur Caroline Gennez moet de cultuur- en erfgoedsector vanaf 1 januari 2027 structureel 47 miljoen euro besparen. Voor de grote landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken – de Hendrik Conscience-erfgoedbibliotheek in Antwerpen, de Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge en de Gentse Boekentoren – betekent dit dat zij 100 procent van hun jaarlijkse Vlaamse subsidies kwijtspelen, een verlies van zo’n 1 miljoen euro. Erkende stadsarchieven en instellingen zoals het AMVB in Brussel zien hun middelen gehalveerd. Vlaanderen vergeet wie zijn geheugen bewaart De abrupte bezuinigingen hebben directe gevolgen voor de aanwas van nieuwe informatieprofessionals. raw_text: De Annie M.G. Schmidtschool is de eerste school in Den Haag die start met de Bibliotheek op school Plus (dBos+). title: includi herontwerpt centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library (GRPL) in Michigan
raw_text: (Meer foto’s onder aan het artikel) Samen met inwoners en medewerkers werkt includi aan de vernieuwing van de centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library in Michigan (VS). Zo ontstaat een uitnodigende bibliotheek die meegroeit met de stad. Het project richt zich op het vernieuwen van de historische entreehal, de jeugdafdelingen en de gemeenschappelijke ruimtes op de benedenverdieping. Deze ruimtes worden getransformeerd tot een hoogwaardige third place: een plek waar mensen graag samenkomen. Hiermee versterkt GRPL haar rol als ontmoetingsplek die inwoners verbindt, waar zij zich thuis voelen en trots op kunnen zijn. Het resultaat wordt een vernieuwde bibliotheek waar iedereen zich welkom voelt. Een plek om boeken te lenen, te studeren, activiteiten bij te wonen of rustig de krant te lezen, alleen of samen met anderen. Een bibliotheek waar mensen willen blijven “We zien bibliotheken als echte third places (derde plekken): laagdrempelige publieke plekken naast huis en werk waar mensen elkaar ontmoeten. Hun deuren staan wijd open en nodigen mensen uit om binnen te komen. Ze bieden het comfort en de sfeer waardoor mensen willen blijven. En ze geven mensen de kans om te groeien. Hoe een bibliotheek eruitziet doet ertoe, maar wat mensen er kunnen doen en beleven is nog belangrijker. title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. title: Buyer group AI in bezwaar en beroep
raw_text: Bezwaar- en beroepsprocessen zijn intensieve trajecten voor overheden. Er zijn grote aantallen dossiers, complexe regelgeving en er komen veel administratieve handelingen bij kijken. AI draagt bij aan efficiëntere processen, betere ondersteuning van medewerkers en snellere dienstverlening aan inwoners en ondernemers. Overheidsorganisaties delen deze processen nog te vaak afzonderlijk in. In de buyer group AI bezwaar en beroep bundelen overheden hun kennis, behoeften en uitdagingen, en treden ze als launching customer op richting de markt. Klankbordgroep: leveranciers gezocht Bouw je AI-oplossingen voor bezwaar en beroep? AIC4NL stelt een klankbordgroep samen van marktpartijen die de gezamenlijke vraag van overheden toetsen aan wat er nu al kan. Onderaan deze pagina lees je hoe je deelneemt. Meld je aan Wat is een buyer group Een buyer group is een groep overheden die rond één proces hun kennis, behoeften en eisen bundelt. Samen brengen ze in kaart waaraan een AI-oplossing moet voldoen: functioneel, juridisch, organisatorisch en technisch. Daarna treden ze richting de markt op als één afnemer, als launching customer . De buyer group werkt in opdracht van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) en valt onder de opschalingsfaciliteit AI van BZK. De uitvoering ligt bij ICTU , de ICT-Uitvoeringsorganisatie van de overheid. AIC4NL coördineert vanuit het werkgebied Digitale Overheid en verbindt overheden, kennisinstellingen en marktpartijen. 39-year-old unvaccinated woman becomes 6th measles death in Pennsylvania
raw_text: A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April. The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman's death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state's health department. In an emailed statement to The Washington Post , the coroner's office said the primary cause of death was listed as "probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles." Epic Games reportedly pivoting to "AI first" game development model
raw_text: Epic Games is shifting to an "AI first" development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That's according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic's Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means "no more hand-written code" and art assets "generated with full AI workflows," according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. Read full article Comments

title: After a 10-year redemption arc, No Man's Sky is coming to the iPhone and iPad
raw_text: Just over 10 years after its initial release, space exploration and survival crafting game No Man's Sky is making its way to the iPhone and iPad, Apple and developer Hello Games announced today. It will run on devices as far back as the iPhone 11 and the third-generation iPad Air. No Man's Sky might not have the most cutting-edge AAA graphics (though they're still strong, and they've come a long way since launch via updates), but the game's uncommon method of generating galaxies of incomprehensible scale on device consistently for all players from a single-seed happening on a phone is remarkable for those of us who remember phones performing far behind consoles or desktop PCs.
